name_en: Da Fo Long Jing (Big Buddha Dragon Well)
processing: Tender shoots are spread, fixed, cooled, dried in stages, sieved and pressed flat in the Long Jing manner, by hand or by machine.
harvest_season: Spring, with the earliest pre-Qingming lots most prized.
appearance_dry: Flat, smooth, straight and pointed blades of a glossy jade green.
appearance_wet: Tender, bright green buds and leaves opening into small clusters.
taste_profile: A tender, lasting aroma with a hint of orchid over a fresh, sweet, mellow taste; sellers also mention chestnut and green pea.

brewing.notes: A glass or a gaiwan both work. Flat leaf floats at first, so give it time, and pour cooler water for tender spring lots.

vintage_note: A current-year tea, like all Long Jing styles: spring harvest of this year, with pre-Qingming lots priced highest, and best within the year. Since 2025 Xinchang has used origin, ecological and premium labels for tracing authentic tea, so look for them on packs.
description:
Da Fo Long Jing comes from Xinchang county in Shaoxing, and takes its name from the county's Big Buddha. It is a Long Jing in style, not West Lake Long Jing in origin, and that is exactly its appeal: the flat-leaf form and nutty character, from a different mountain.

The tea is mainly grown above 400 metres in Xinchang's hills. Young shoots are spread, fixed, cooled, dried in stages and pressed flat, which gives the smooth, pointed blades and a highland freshness.

Expect a clean, tender aroma with a hint of orchid and a sweet, fresh, mellow cup. As with other Long Jing, water around 80 degrees and a short first steep protect the sweetness; boiling water brings out a bitter edge.

It is sold by spring harvest and grade. Because Long Jing names cause confusion, make sure the pack says Xinchang and shows a harvest date, and compare it side by side with a West Lake lot to learn what you are paying for.
history:
Xinchang's tea lost much of its reputation in the 1980s, and from the 1990s the county's growers moved from round-shaped to flat-leaf tea. Several local names appeared along the way before they were consolidated as Da Fo Long Jing.

The tea won the only gold award at a Chinese science and technology products fair in 1995, and a standard for it was drawn up in 1997. It later gained protected-origin status, and in 2025 the county introduced labels to trace and protect authentic tea.
